question: Can training, emergence, grokking, scaling laws, and mechanistic algorithms be unified as motion on a graph of interpretable internal heuristic models?

key_findings.claim: The semantic landscape is defined over heuristic models—well-formed internal algorithms—rather than raw weights, with fallibility measuring expected prediction error over the data distribution.
key_findings.evidence: The central conjecture posits mappings from parameter subsets to formulas in a formal language; many weight states can correspond to the same heuristic model, and graph edges represent transitions enabled by training data.

key_findings.claim: Grokking is modeled as first passage across semantic barriers from memorization to a low-fallibility generalizing algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: Dataset size controls graph connectivity; below a critical size the memorization and generalization nodes disconnect, while above it the proposed grokking rate is proportional to D minus Dc and grokking time scales as its inverse.

key_findings.claim: Emergence with parameter scale is described as node percolation: a larger network can formulate intermediate algorithms that open a path to a previously inaccessible capability.
key_findings.evidence: With data assumed sufficient, parameter count controls which heuristic-model nodes exist; crossing a capacity threshold connects low-fallibility states and creates abrupt behavioral change.

key_findings.claim: A phenomenological semantic trap model derives power-law fallibility in training steps, dataset size, and parameter count.
key_findings.evidence: Assuming exponentially distributed barriers, activated hopping, and fallibility inverse in successful barrier crossings yields F(S) proportional to S^-mu, F(D) proportional to D^-mu, and F(N) proportional to N raised to -mu/(df alpha). It predicts equal data and time exponents.

key_findings.claim: The theory argues that capability emergence should be judged through internal algorithm change rather than an abrupt external metric alone.
key_findings.evidence: In response to the metric-mirage critique, the paper notes metrics can hide or manufacture discontinuities and proposes mechanistic interpretation of learned representations as the deciding evidence.

key_findings.claim: Most central objects and scaling assumptions are posited rather than constructed or empirically validated.
key_findings.evidence: The paper provides no algorithm mapping weights to formal heuristic models, no measured semantic graph or barrier distribution, and no new training experiments testing percolation thresholds or equal exponents. Exponential barriers, Arrhenius rates, and inverse-fallibility progress are phenomenological choices.

method.core_idea: Coarse-grain neural training into a graph trajectory among interpretable algorithms and import percolation, random-walk, and glassy-trap models to explain qualitative and quantitative learning phenomena.
method.mechanism: Data adds edges between heuristic models, parameters add available nodes, and optimization crosses fallibility barriers. Connectivity transitions yield grokking and capability emergence; an exponential barrier ensemble and activated hopping produce heavy-tailed waiting times and scaling laws.
assumptions: Network parameters admit useful mappings to well-formed internal algorithms.
Fallibility is intrinsic to a heuristic model and independent of data and parameter scale.
Dataset size primarily controls graph degree and parameter count primarily controls node availability.
Barrier heights are exponentially distributed and transition rates are Arrhenius-like.
Average fallibility decreases inversely with the number of successful semantic barrier crossings.

techniques.role: Defines interpretable internal computations as nodes in a coarse-grained state space.
Assigns expected predictive error to heuristic models independently of weight coordinates.
Explains critical dataset size and grokking time through connectivity.
Explains abrupt capabilities when scale makes intermediate algorithms representable.
Derives power laws from activated motion through exponentially distributed barriers.

evaluations.setting: Analytical reinterpretation of reported grokking experiments.
evaluations.metric: Critical dataset size, transient loss barrier, and grokking-time dependence on data.
evaluations.result: The percolation picture reproduces a proposed t_g proportional to 1/(D-Dc) relation qualitatively consistent with cited work.
evaluations.baseline: Weight-norm, circuit-formation, and phase-transition explanations from prior literature.

evaluations.setting: Conceptual account of capability emergence with model size.
evaluations.metric: Existence of an accessible path to a low-fallibility heuristic model.
evaluations.result: Node availability produces a threshold in principle, but no concrete model graph or checkpoint series is measured.
evaluations.baseline: Empirical emergent-ability reports and the quantization model.

evaluations.setting: Semantic trap model in asymptotic data, parameter, and training-step regimes.
evaluations.result: The model permits separate parameter exponent and equal dataset/time exponents through barrier and graph-dynamics parameters.
evaluations.baseline: Observed neural scaling laws and the quantization model's skill-frequency derivation.

limitations: No operational algorithm extracts heuristic models, graph edges, or semantic barriers from weights.
No new empirical experiment tests the percolation or trap-model predictions.
The formal-language mapping conjecture is broad enough to be non-identifying without constraints on semantics and granularity.
Data, parameters, optimizer, and architecture may jointly change both nodes and edges rather than factor cleanly.
Many barrier distributions and progress rules can generate power laws, weakening falsifiability without independent measurements.
failure_modes: Different coarse-grainings can produce incompatible semantic graphs for the same network.
A smooth representation change can look like node emergence after arbitrary discretization.
Benchmark thresholds can be caused by nonlinear metrics rather than percolation.
Training may revise several interacting algorithms at once, violating single-node hopping and inverse-progress assumptions.
The fitted scaling exponents may be explained post hoc by free graph dimension and dynamical parameters.
reusable_insights: Track learned algorithms over training rather than inferring emergence solely from aggregate loss.
Separate representability of a capability from optimizer access to it.
Model data scarcity as missing learning transitions and capacity scarcity as missing internal states, then test that factorization.
Demand an operational coarse-graining before treating an appealing physical analogy as explanatory theory.
open_questions: Can mechanistic interpretability construct a reproducible semantic graph for a nontrivial training run?
Are semantic barrier heights exponential when measured from interventions between identified circuits?
Do dataset and training-time scaling exponents match after controlling compute and optimization?
Can percolation predict a capability threshold prospectively rather than explain it after observation?

competitive_landscape.title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest unified theory of discrete learned skills, scaling laws, and emergence.
competitive_landscape.difference: The quantization model derives scaling from power-law skill-use frequencies and tests decomposed gradients; semantic landscapes derive it from graph geometry and barriers but lack comparable empirical extraction.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary empirical phenomenon the semantic percolation account seeks to explain.
competitive_landscape.difference: Power et al. establish delayed generalization and critical conditions experimentally; this paper recasts the transition as first passage on a data-connected algorithm graph.

competitive_landscape.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary empirical catalog of abrupt capability changes with model scale.
competitive_landscape.difference: Wei et al. characterize benchmark thresholds; semantic landscapes propose that new representable nodes connect paths to low-fallibility algorithms.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct competing metric-based explanation of apparent discontinuities.
competitive_landscape.difference: The mirage paper shows nonlinear metrics can turn smooth improvement into jumps; semantic landscapes concede that point but reserve 'emergence' for a mechanistically verified new internal algorithm.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The semantic landscape provides a unified statistical-physics framework for grokking, capability emergence, neural scaling laws, and mechanistic interpretability through trajectories on a graph of learned algorithms.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The node-versus-edge distinction and mechanistic definition of emergence are conceptually productive. As a theory it remains pre-operational: key mappings and barrier statistics are assumed, flexible exponents are not independently constrained, and no experiment distinguishes it from quantization, metric, or weight-space alternatives.

reviewer_notes: Read the complete 14-page extraction, including formal definitions, both percolation arguments, full trap-model derivation, quantization comparison, mechanistic agenda, and scaling critique. Four direct primary arXiv alternatives and empirical anchors were checked on 2026-08-23.
